findings.quote: it advised the envoys whom the Achaeans regularly sent from time to time to pay close attention and to show the reception that was fitting
findings.problem: Greek: τοῖς δὲ πρεσβευταῖς τοῖς αἰεὶ παρ᾽ ἑαυτῶν ἐκπεμπομένοις παρῄνει προσέχειν τὸν νοῦν καὶ καταδοχὴν ποιεῖσθαι τὴν ἁρμόζουσαν. The subject is the senate; παρ᾽ ἑαυτῶν means 'from the senate's own side', so the envoys are the ones Rome sends out. The dative recipients (τοῖς ... πρεσβευταῖς, with the infinitives) are the Achaeans being advised to pay attention and give a fitting reception to Roman envoys, just as the Romans receive envoys who come to them (καθάπερ καὶ Ῥωμαῖοι ποιοῦνται τῶν παραγινομένων πρὸς αὐτοὺς πρεσβευτῶν). The current English makes them Achaean envoys, which inverts the sense. Note: strictly the dative τοῖς πρεσβευταῖς is the object of προσέχειν (pay attention to the envoys), with Achaeans as understood addressees.
findings.proposed_fix: it advised the Achaeans to pay close attention to the envoys whom it sent out from time to time and to give them the reception that was fitting

units.note: Greek breaks off mid-word (ἄχρι τού) at chapter end; it is completed at the start of ch. 14 (του προβάντες ἔλυσαν). The English closing clause 'so the first interview ended there' translates across that seam correctly. Bracketed Greek (πεπεισμένος ... φόβον) is an editorial deletion, not a lacuna; English sense is accurate either way.

findings.quote: the man who had actually carried out the deed, so that the senate, as they said, might learn the facts from him
findings.problem: Greek: τὸν αὐθέντην γεγονότα τῆς πράξεως, ὡς ἐκεῖνοί φασιν, ἵνα πύθηται παρὰ τούτου τὰς ἀληθείας ἡ σύγκλητος. 'ὡς ἐκεῖνοί φασιν' (as they [Appius and colleagues] say) qualifies the claim that Cassander was the author of the deed, not the purpose clause. English attaches 'as they said' to the senate's learning the facts.
findings.proposed_fix: the man who, as they said, had been the author of the deed, so that the senate might learn the truth from him

units.note: Opening clause: Greek reads κατὰ πάντα τρόπον ἐλαττούμενοι Γορτύνιοι τοὺς Κνωσίους, with a passive participle (ἐλαττούμενοι, 'being worsted/at a disadvantage') governing an accusative; this is grammatically suspect and probably corrupt or in need of emendation (sense wanted is the Gortynians getting the better of / disadvantaging Cnossians, as the territorial cuts show). The English 'doing everything possible to weaken the Cnossians' silently resolves this; the ambiguity ought to be flagged but I propose no fix. The *** lacuna before ἀπέκτεινα τοὺς περὶ Μενοίτιον is marked in the English ('after a gap in the text'); subject of the killing is unknown. Remainder checked and accurate.

findings.quote: Calling him king and offspring of gods, they said that if he abused such a name he might perhaps obtain some pity and pardon for what had happened
findings.problem: Greek is a badly damaged papyrus text: βασιλέα καὶ θ̣ε̣ω̣ν̣ α̣ι̣μ̣α̣ τοῦτον λέγοντες καταχρώμενοι τ̣ε̣υ̣ξ̣ε̣σ̣θ̣α̣ι̣ τινος ἐλέους καὶ συγγνώμης ἐπὶ τῳ... σασθαι τ̣ο̣ν̣ β̣α̣σ̣ι̣λεα... Only 'calling this man king and blood (αἷμα) of gods', '[to] obtain some pity and pardon' and 'the king' survive. The conditional 'if he abused such a name', 'perhaps' and 'for what had happened' are not in the Greek; the lacunae are silently smoothed into a complete sentence.
findings.proposed_fix: Calling him king and 'blood of gods' [text lost] ... [that he would] obtain some pity and pardon [text lost] ... the king ...

findings.quote: yet it would have been more kingly not to be the first to break faith, but rather to let others violate agreements before he did so himself
findings.problem: Greek: ων γε μὴν καὶ βασιλικώτερος.... ονων ων ἀθετηθῆναι γὰρ υ̣φ̣ ε̣τ̣ε̣ρων κ̣ρ̣ε̣ι̣τ̣τ̣ον ἦν ἢ πρότερον αὐτὸν ἀθετεῖν τὰς πίστεις καὶ μὴν ἀδικεῖσθαι μᾶλλον η... Only 'more kingly' (βασιλικώτερος) survives before a gap; the surviving clause is 'for it was better to be betrayed by others than himself first to break his pledges', followed by 'and indeed to be wronged rather than ...' (broken off). English invents 'yet it would have been more kingly' as a whole judgment and omits the following 'to be wronged rather than' clause.
findings.proposed_fix: ... and more kingly still [text lost] ... for it was better to be betrayed by others than to be the first himself to break his pledges; and indeed to be wronged rather than [text lost] ...

findings.quote: They said that all men admire Philip for his greatness of spirit
findings.problem: Greek: ... ς θαυμάζουσι μὲν πάντες Φίλιππον διὰ τὴν ορ [gap] ... ς μεγαλοψυχίαν. 'They said' is not in the Greek (it is in the damaged lead-in only), and there are gaps both before θαυμάζουσι and between 'διὰ τὴν ορ' and 'μεγαλοψυχίαν' (a lost qualifier of the greatness of spirit); the English reads on as whole.
findings.proposed_fix: [text lost] ... all men admire Philip for his [text lost] ... greatness of spirit

findings.quote: Ptolemy, by contrast, bound the men naked to carts
findings.problem: Greek: *** πλὴν ὅγε Πτολεμαῖος δήσας τοὺς ἀνθρώπους γυμνοὺς ταῖς ἁμάξαις εἷλκε. The sentence is preceded by a marked lacuna (***); πλὴν ὅγε means 'except that Ptolemy, for his part', and the identity of the 'men' is lost with the gap. English smooths the gap into a continuous contrast.
findings.proposed_fix: [text lost] ... except that Ptolemy for his part bound the men naked to carts

units.note: Whole chapter is fragmentary (papyrus, with partial letters and gaps). Material wholly omitted from the English: the gnomic lines 'ἔγγιστα τῆς θείας φύσεως εἶναι' ('nearest to the divine nature') and 'θεὸς γὰρ οὐδεὶς πρότερος κακῶς ποιεῖ τοὺς ανους...' ('for no god is the first to do harm to ...'), plus the clause 'τυγχάνειν τιμῶν' ('to receive honours'). The Chaeronea sentence and the 'imitate least of all' sentence are accurate. The speaker and the 'they' of the fragment are unidentifiable; the English should mark gaps rather than supply a narrative.
